bridge_line: Our greatest teacher and reader of Scripture. Later ages argued over how far he went.

dates.note: In-build attestation (T3-E): alexforce1A3 places "Origen's peak c. 220s-230s" and alexforce3B1 dates the Origen-Demetrius conflict to c. 230s CE. Bounds his peak activity in THIS world, not his life - he outlived his Alexandrian period, and no birth or death date is attested in this build.

bridge_line: An early teacher here who wrote for educated readers coming to the faith.

dates.note: In-build attestation (T3-E): alexcore001's own time_window note fixes "Clement's Alexandrian activity c. 180s-202 as the earliest richly-attested formation activity", and alexforce1A3 has him arriving c. 180. Bounds his activity in this world, not his life.

bridge_line: Bishop of Alexandria. He wrote the life of Antony.
A student who wrote a farewell speech describing how Origen taught.
A blind teacher here, known for holding whole books in memory.

dates.note: UNVERIFIED (T3-E): reference-work lookup 2026-08-15 (Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Didymus the Blind"), NOT verified against a primary edition. This build dates only Palladius's Lausiac History (c. 419-420, alexstory002), the source of its Didymus material, not Didymus himself. Scholar recheck required.

bridge_line: A visitor from outside who wrote down what he saw of Egypt's teachers.
Bishop of Alexandria, who fell out with Origen and drove him from the city.
The earliest teacher our school remembers by name. Only the name is kept.

dates.display: head of the Alexandrian school from c. 180, still living 193, died c. 200
dates.note: UNVERIFIED (T3-E): reference-work lookup 2026-08-15 (Catholic Encyclopedia, "Pantaenus", citing Eusebius Hist. eccl. V.x and Chron. Abr. 2210), NOT verified against those editions directly. alexcore001 calls him "boundary-adjacent" to this world's horizon but attests no dates for him, and this record's own bridge_line says only the name is kept. Scholar recheck required.

bridge_line: The evangelist our city claims as its founder. The claim is a later tradition.
The Egyptian monk whose life Athanasius wrote.
